title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 26
paragraphs: On August 25, the eve of the battle of Borodino, Monsieur de Beausset, prefect of the French Emperor's palace, arrived at Napoleon's quarters at Valuevo with Colonel Fabvier—the former from Paris, the latter from Madrid.

Putting on his court uniform, Monsieur de Beausset ordered a box he had brought for the Emperor to be carried before him and entered the first compartment of Napoleon's tent, where he began opening the box while chatting with Napoleon's aides-de-camp.
Fabvier did not enter the tent but stayed at the entrance talking to some generals he knew.

Emperor Napoleon had not yet left his bedroom and was finishing his morning grooming. Snorting and grunting slightly, he presented now his back and now his plump, hairy chest to the brush with which his valet was rubbing him down. Another valet, with his finger over the mouth of a bottle, was sprinkling Eau de Cologne on the Emperor's pampered body with an expression that seemed to say he alone knew where and how much cologne should be applied. Napoleon's short hair was wet and matted on his forehead, but his face, though puffy and yellow, expressed physical satisfaction. "Go on, harder, go on!" he muttered to the valet rubbing him, slightly twitching and grunting. An aide-de-camp, who had come to report the number of prisoners taken in yesterday's action, was standing by the door after delivering his message, awaiting permission to withdraw. Napoleon, frowning, looked at him from under his brows.

"No prisoners!" he said, repeating the aide's words. "They are forcing us to exterminate them. So much the worse for the Russian army... Go on... harder, harder!" he muttered, hunching his back and presenting his fat shoulders.
"All right. Send in Monsieur de Beausset, and Fabvier too," he said, nodding to the aide-de-camp.
"Yes, sire," and the aide vanished through the tent door.
Two valets quickly dressed His Majesty, and wearing the blue uniform of the Guards, he walked with firm, rapid steps to the reception area.

De Beausset's hands meanwhile were busy arranging the present he had brought from the Empress on two chairs directly facing the entrance. But Napoleon had dressed and come out so unexpectedly fast that de Beausset hadn't had time to finish preparing the surprise.

Napoleon noticed at once what they were up to and guessed they weren't ready. Not wanting to deprive them of the pleasure of surprising him, he pretended not to see de Beausset and called Fabvier over, listening silently and with a stern frown to Fabvier's account of the heroism and devotion of the troops fighting at Salamanca, at the other end of Europe, with but one thought—to be worthy of their Emperor—and but one fear—to displease him. The result of that battle had been disastrous. Napoleon made ironic remarks during Fabvier's report, as if he had never expected matters to go otherwise in his absence.
"I must make up for that in Moscow," said Napoleon. "I'll see you later," he added, and summoned de Beausset, who by then had prepared the surprise, covering something on the chairs with a cloth.
De Beausset made a deep bow—that courtly French bow which only the old servants of the Bourbons knew how to make—and approached, presenting an envelope.
Napoleon turned to him cheerfully and pulled his ear.
"You've hurried here. I'm very glad. Well, what is Paris saying?" he asked, suddenly changing his former stern expression to one of great cordiality.
"Sire, all Paris regrets your absence," replied de Beausset, as was expected.
But though Napoleon knew de Beausset had to say something like this, and though in his lucid moments he knew it was untrue, he was pleased to hear it. Again he honored him by touching his ear.
"I'm very sorry to have made you travel so far," he said.
"Sire, I expected nothing less than to find you at the gates of Moscow," replied de Beausset.
Napoleon smiled and, raising his head absent-mindedly, glanced to the right. An aide approached with gliding steps and offered him a gold snuffbox, which he took.

"Yes, it has worked out well for you," he said, raising the open snuffbox to his nose. "You love to travel, and in three days you will see Moscow. You surely didn't expect to see that Asiatic capital. You will have a pleasant trip."
De Beausset bowed gratefully at this acknowledgment of his taste for travel (of which he had not till then been aware).
"Ha, what's this?" asked Napoleon, noticing that all the courtiers were looking at something hidden under a cloth.
With courtly skill, de Beausset half-turned and, without showing his back to the Emperor, stepped back two paces, whisked off the cloth, and said:
"A present to Your Majesty from the Empress."
It was a portrait, painted in bright colors by Gerard, of the son born to Napoleon by the daughter of the Emperor of Austria—the boy whom everyone for some reason called "the King of Rome."

A very pretty curly-haired boy with a look of the Christ child in the Sistine Madonna was depicted playing with a stick and ball. The ball represented the globe and the stick in his other hand a scepter.

Though it was not entirely clear what the artist meant by showing the so-called King of Rome stabbing the earth with a stick, the allegory apparently seemed to Napoleon—as it had to everyone who had seen it in Paris—perfectly clear and very pleasing.
"The King of Rome!" he said, pointing to the portrait with a graceful gesture. "Admirable!"

With the natural ability of an Italian to change his facial expression at will, he stepped closer to the portrait and assumed a look of pensive tenderness. He felt that what he now said and did would be historic, and it seemed best for him—whose greatness enabled his son to play ball with the globe—to display, in contrast to that grandeur, the simplest paternal tenderness. His eyes grew misty, he stepped forward, glanced around for a chair (which seemed to place itself beneath him), and sat down before the portrait. At a single gesture, everyone tiptoed out, leaving the great man alone with his emotion.

After sitting still for a while, he touched—himself not knowing why—the thick spot of paint representing the highest highlight in the portrait, rose, and sent for de Beausset and the officer on duty. He ordered the portrait to be carried outside his tent so that the Old Guard stationed around it might have the pleasure of seeing the King of Rome, the son and heir of their adored monarch.

And while he was doing Monsieur de Beausset the honor of breakfasting with him, they heard—as Napoleon had anticipated—the rapturous cries of the officers and men of the Old Guard who had rushed to see the portrait.
"Long live the Emperor! Long live the King of Rome! Long live the Emperor!" came the ecstatic cries.
After breakfast, Napoleon dictated his order of the day to the army in de Beausset's presence.
"Short and energetic!" he remarked when he had read over the proclamation he had dictated straight off without corrections. It ran:

Soldiers! This is the battle you have so longed for. Victory depends on you. It is essential for us; it will give us all we need: comfortable quarters and a speedy return to our country. Behave as you did at Austerlitz, Friedland, Vitebsk, and Smolensk. Let our remotest posterity recall your achievements this day with pride. Let it be said of each of you: "He was in the great battle before Moscow!"
"Before Moscow!" repeated Napoleon, and inviting Monsieur de Beausset, who was so fond of travel, to accompany him on his ride, he went out to where the horses stood saddled.
"Your Majesty is too kind!" replied de Beausset to the invitation; he wanted to sleep, couldn't ride, and was afraid of trying.
But Napoleon nodded to the traveler, and de Beausset had to mount. When Napoleon came out of the tent, the cheering of the Guards before his son's portrait grew still louder. Napoleon frowned.
"Take him away!" he said, pointing with a gracefully majestic gesture to the portrait. "It is too soon for him to see a battlefield."
De Beausset closed his eyes, bowed his head, and sighed deeply, to show how profoundly he appreciated the Emperor's words.
